episodes.title: Lynching of Rube Carothers
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Rube Carothers took place on the night of August 16, 1880, near Greenvine, Texas, when masked men took Carothers, a Black man accused of selling stolen cattle, from the guards holding him during his preliminary examination and hanged him from a cottonwood tree. A coroner's jury found that he had been hanged by persons unknown. Wire reports carried the killing nationally, while the Brenham Weekly Banner printed a local letter and the presiding justice's statement.

episodes.title: Lynching of two Black men at May's Lick, Kentucky
episodes.summary: The lynching of two Black men at May's Lick, Kentucky, took place in early August 1880, after the two, unnamed in every report, were accused of fatally shooting Perry Jefferson of May's Lick on August 3. According to a special telegram from Flemingsburg, the men were caught and lynched soon after the shooting. The story was known only from that one dispatch, which the Cincinnati wire said carried "no further particulars," but it was reprinted as a brief in papers from Pennsylvania to California.

episodes.title: Lynching of Reed Evans
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of Reed Evans took place at Pennington, Trinity County, Texas, about 1 August 1880, when a party of armed men took Evans, a Black youth, from the jail and hanged him. Evans was being held on a charge of killing a white boy of about twelve, whom he said he had shot by accident. The hanging was reported in telegraphic briefs and crime digests across the country, and an Austin weekly explained it as the act of a mob that thought him too young for judicial punishment.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Washington (Denver, Tennessee)
episodes.summary: The lynching of George Washington was the hanging of a Black man by a mob in Tennessee, reported in early August 1880. According to a Kentucky paper, Washington was taken from the jail at Denver, Tennessee, and lynched for the murder of Egbert Fagan. The case reached readers mainly as a one-line item in crime roundups printed in the Midwest.

episodes.title: Lynching of Green Ellis
episodes.summary: The lynching of Green Ellis took place on the night of August 26, 1880, when a mob of armed men took Ellis, a Black man held under guard at Guthrie, Kentucky, and hanged him near the town. Ellis had been accused of knocking a white woman, Mrs. Duncan, from her horse, beating her and robbing her of $12. Wire dispatches carried the story to papers across the country within two days, with estimates of the mob ranging from twenty-five to more than one hundred men.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Diggs
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Diggs took place shortly before dawn on 27 July 1880, when about fifty men forced the jail at Rockville, Maryland, took Diggs, a Black man, from the sheriff and hanged him on the road toward Darnestown. Diggs had been arrested the night before, accused of assaulting Mrs. James Tschiffely, a white woman, near Darnestown. The story ran in short wire briefs across the country, and Democratic and other white editors cited it in arguments over Southern violence.

episodes.title: Lynching of an unnamed Black man in Webster Parish, Louisiana (1880)
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The lynching of an unnamed Black man in Webster Parish, Louisiana, was a killing reported in the national press in August 1880, in which a number of citizens took a prisoner accused of murdering his wife from the officers holding him and shot him to death. The only account, a brief miscellany item, said the man was struck by more than twenty bullets and that none of the parties' names were known.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Alexander Ellison
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Alexander Ellison took place at Woodland Mills, Obion County, Tennessee, in early August 1880, after Ellison, a Black man, shot a white man named Harry Crenshaw on the night of Sunday, August 1. Wire dispatches said a crowd was pursuing Ellison to lynch him and that he was expected to be lynched after his arrest, and the story ran in papers from Washington to Dallas. A nearby Kentucky paper reported a week later that Ellison was in jail at Troy and that a report of his hanging was untrue.

episodes.title: Attack on Joshua Mack near Columbus, Indiana
episodes.summary: The attack on Joshua Mack near Columbus, Indiana, was a night raid on August 11, 1880, in which masked men broke into the house of Mack, a Black man, threatened to hang him and ordered him to leave the county. Mack was released on a promise to leave but resolved to stay, and papers reported the attack as part of election-season efforts to drive Black residents out of Indiana.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Tobe Bell and Louis Rosenberg
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Tobe Bell and Louis Rosenberg took place in Yazoo county, Mississippi, in late July 1880, when a crowd gathered to lynch the two men arrested for the killing of Dr. Wiley T. Williams of Mechanicsburg. Deputy sheriffs moved the prisoners out of the crowd's reach, and both men were later committed to jail without bail. Mississippi papers credited the deputy's quick action, while the wire copy that ran across the country mentioned only the assassination and a confession.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Thomas Smith
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Thomas Smith occurred at Burlingame, Osage County, Kansas, in August 1880, when townspeople threatened to lynch Smith, a Black man held for a shooting that killed Wesley Thomas and mortally wounded a saloon keeper named Baker. The sheriff took Smith away by train through a large crowd at the depot, and no attack on him was reported. Telegraph reports of the shooting ran in papers across the country, but only the Emporia News mentioned the threats of lynching.

episodes.title: Lynching at Winnsborough, Louisiana (1880)
episodes.summary: The lynching at Winnsborough, Louisiana, was the hanging in late July 1880 of an unnamed seventeen-year-old Black youth, taken from the Franklin Parish jail by "a body of men" and hanged to a tree outside the town. He had been jailed on an accusation of attempting to "outrage" the daughter of a prominent lawyer, and the episode is known only from a short item in an Alexandria weekly quoting a New Orleans dispatch.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John Robinson
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of John Robinson took place near Hagerstown, Maryland, in August 1880, when Robinson, a Black man, was captured after leaving a farm near Clearspring with the wife and five children of a white farmer named Key. According to a Baltimore dispatch, there were threats of lynching him, but he was safely jailed at Hagerstown. Papers in Washington, Memphis and West Virginia carried the case as a short news item.

episodes.title: Jonesboro attack on the Thompson family
episodes.summary: The Jonesboro attack on the Thompson family was a night raid by about fifteen disguised white men on the cabin of Joe Thompson, a Black farm worker near Jonesboro, Clayton County, Georgia, around midnight on July 28, 1880. The raiders flogged Thompson and his wife, killed his daughter Millie Johnson and wounded his son Bob, reportedly in revenge for Thompson's prosecution of a white man. Militia guarded the arrested suspects, and Northern papers presented the killing as a revival of Ku-Klux terror in a presidential campaign.

episodes.title: Killing of Barney Cleveland
episodes.summary: The killing of Barney Cleveland was the fatal shooting of a Black barber from Moline by a special officer at Milan on August 7, 1880, while the officer was trying to arrest him. Cleveland died two days later, and a coroner's jury found the shooting a justifiable homicide by an officer in the discharge of his duty. The Rock Island Argus followed the case closely and defended the officer, while denouncing local Republicans whom it accused of making Cleveland's race a partisan issue at the inquest.

episodes.title: Wilmington mobbing of John H. Harris
episodes.summary: The Wilmington mobbing of John H. Harris was the pursuit of a Black Democratic campaign speaker from Virginia by a crowd through the streets of Wilmington, Delaware, on the evening of August 3, 1880, after he spoke at City Hall. Policemen met him and escorted him to the railroad depot, and no injury to him was reported. Democratic papers as far away as Texas and Kentucky retold it as Republicans denying free speech to a Black Democrat.

episodes.title: Warning notices to Black residents of Bluffton, Indiana
episodes.summary: The warning notices to Black residents of Bluffton, Indiana, were anonymous cards sent in late July and early August 1880 that told the town's few Black residents to leave and warned white residents to get rid of the Black people they employed or housed. No violence was reported, but Republican-leaning papers cited the warnings during the 1880 campaign as Democratic "Ku-Klux" intimidation.

episodes.title: Cherokee mobilization against Creek freedmen at Fort Gibson
episodes.summary: The Cherokee mobilization against Creek freedmen at Fort Gibson was an armed gathering of several hundred Cherokees in early August 1880 that demanded the surrender of thirteen Black men of the Creek Nation and threatened to go after them. The thirteen were accused of crossing into the Cherokee Nation and shooting two Cherokee youths, Cobb and Cowan, to avenge the hanging of two Creek Black men. A council at Muskogee defused the confrontation on August 4; the story ran nationally as a clash of 'Creek negroes' and Cherokees.

episodes.title: Cochran cabin shooting
episodes.summary: The Cochran cabin shooting was a night attack by a disguised party of young white men on the cabin of John Brown, a Black man living near Cochran, Georgia, in August 1880, in which Brown killed two of the attackers, brothers named Dykes, with a shotgun. A coroner's jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide. Northern papers reported it as a Black man's defense of his home and remarked on the Southern jury's verdict.

episodes.title: Threats against the Blackville Republican meeting (1880)
episodes.summary: The threats against the Blackville Republican meeting were published calls in July 1880 by Democratic newspapers in Barnwell County, South Carolina, for Democratic clubs to attend a Republican ratification meeting at Blackville, which Republican papers read as a summons to break it up. The meeting, held on July 27, was later reported to have drawn more than 4,000 people and to have passed without disturbance. Northern Republican papers nonetheless cited the episode as evidence of "bulldozing" in the 1880 campaign, while Democratic papers used its peaceful outcome to ridicule those warnings.

episodes.title: Reported intimidation of Black residents at Shelbyville, Indiana (1880)
episodes.summary: The reported intimidation of Black residents at Shelbyville, Indiana, was one of several "attempts at intimidation" named in a Cincinnati dispatch of August 12, 1880, during the presidential campaign. The dispatch gave no details of what happened there, and it is the only report of the episode found.

episodes.title: Threat letter to J. T. Allen
episodes.summary: The threat letter to J. T. Allen was an anonymous note left at the home of Allen, a Black Democrat in Cairo, Illinois, in August 1880, warning that he would be tarred, feathered and drummed out of town unless he left the Democratic clubs. No attack followed in the coverage, which comes only from the Democratic Cairo Bulletin, which printed the letter as evidence of Republican "bulldozing" during the campaign.

episodes.title: McGhee's Switch election intimidation
episodes.summary: The McGhee's Switch election intimidation took place at the Precinct No. 9 polling place at McGhee's Switch, Montgomery County, Alabama, on the night of the state election of August 2, 1880, when a militia company and an armed posse came to the polls and the Black Republican inspector, A. Oliver, was forced out of the vote count. Republican accounts said the ballot box was refilled in the dark after a candle was knocked over, producing a return of 540 Democratic votes. Northern Republican papers made it a leading example of Alabama election fraud; the militia's commander denied any intimidation.

episodes.title: Shannondale picnic killings
episodes.summary: The Shannondale picnic killings were two deaths at Shannondale, Chariton County, Missouri, on or about 28 August 1880, when one Black man shot another dead after a quarrel at a picnic and a constable then killed the shooter with a shotgun as he resisted arrest. The story reached papers across the country through a Sedalia telegram that told it entirely from the officer's side, and the officer's name and the timing of the shootings differ between versions.

episodes.title: Coffeeville riot of 1880
episodes.summary: The Coffeeville riot of 1880 was a street fight in Coffeeville, Yalobusha County, Mississippi, on August 21, 1880, between R. V. Pearson, the Greenback candidate for sheriff, and Spearman, a Black man marching in a Democratic procession. Early wire reports said Pearson killed Spearman instantly and was himself shot dead, but later Mississippi reports had Spearman only slightly wounded and Pearson recovering to win the sheriff's election three days later. Democratic and Greenback papers blamed each other's side for starting it.

episodes.title: Dixon account of political intimidation in Yazoo
episodes.summary: The Dixon account of political intimidation in Yazoo was a disputed report, carried by Northern Republican newspapers in August 1880, that white Democrats in Yazoo County, Mississippi, had warned F. P. Dixon against supporting James A. Garfield and were breaking up gatherings of Black men to stop political talk. Dixon was the brother of H. M. Dixon, whose earlier killing in Yazoo was blamed on James Barksdale. Governor J. M. Stone, Yazoo City officials and the editors of the Yazoo Herald denied the account as false, and no violence during the visit was reported by either side.

episodes.title: Huntsville election-day assault on Black voters (1880)
episodes.summary: The Huntsville election-day assault on Black voters was an attack on a line of Black men marching to the polls in Huntsville, Alabama, during the state election of August 1880. According to letters sent to Washington, a white Democrat clubbed the voters with a cane, severely wounding one man, striking several others and dispersing them. Republican papers in the North printed the letters as evidence that intimidation and fraud had produced the large Democratic majority in Alabama.

episodes.title: Expulsion of a Black man from Lewistown (1880)
episodes.summary: The expulsion of a Black man from Lewistown was an incident in the summer of 1880 or earlier in which an unnamed "colored man" was pelted with rotten eggs and driven out of town after being accused of insulting a white woman on the street. It is known only through an exchange between two newspaper editors over whether the act resembled the expulsions of Black people in the South.

episodes.title: Killing of Dave Ball
episodes.summary: The killing of Dave Ball was the shooting of a Black man near Senatobia, Tate County, Mississippi, in August 1880 by W. R. McNorton, who had been keeping watch for him at a house. Ball was accused of trying to enter the rooms of women in the house, and a coroner's jury ruled the killing justifiable homicide. A Jackson weekly printed the story as "Got What He Deserved."

episodes.title: Shooting of Frank Bowie
episodes.summary: The shooting of Frank Bowie occurred on a Tuesday afternoon in 1880, reported at the end of August, at LaVilla, Florida, when Deputy Sheriff McCallum shot Bowie, a Black man, in the leg as he fled an attempted arrest. Bowie survived and was taken home for medical care, while the LaVilla town marshal arrested the deputy for firing his pistol in the street.

episodes.title: Stoning of John H. Harris at New Castle, Delaware
episodes.summary: The stoning of John H. Harris was an attack on a Black Democratic campaign speaker from Virginia at New Castle, Delaware, on the night of Saturday, July 31, 1880, when missiles were thrown at him from a crowd as he spoke outside the courthouse. The stone missed Harris but severely wounded a white bystander, and Harris spent the night under the sheriff's protection. Delaware papers attributed the attack to Black listeners opposed to a Black man speaking for the Democrats, and Democratic papers across the country used it as an answer to Republican reports of Southern outrages.

episodes.title: Danville camp meeting riot
episodes.summary: The Danville camp meeting riot was a series of attacks by white men on a colored Baptist camp meeting at Danville, about ten miles south of Hillsboro in Highland County, Ohio, in late July 1880. Attackers driven off at night returned in larger numbers on Sunday, broke up the meeting, and reportedly fired on worshippers leaving in wagons. One white attacker, William Dickman, died of a gunshot wound; reported Black deaths were never confirmed. Papers outside Ohio made the attack a point in the 1880 campaign, and the Hillsboro paper answered that Danville was a Democratic township.

episodes.title: Beating of Black voters at the Memphis First ward polls
episodes.summary: The beating of Black voters at the Memphis First ward polls took place on August 5, 1880, when a crowd at the First ward polling place in Memphis, Tennessee, attacked about twenty-five Black men during the Shelby County election. The only account, in the Memphis Public Ledger, blamed the men for trying to keep white voters from the ballot box and said no one was seriously injured, although the same page reported that a Black coal-yard worker, Dick Lyles, was left insensible in the street. Outside Memphis, reports of the election described it as peaceful and did not mention the fighting.

episodes.title: East Baton Rouge church attack
episodes.summary: The East Baton Rouge church attack was an assault in April 1880 in which a crowd of white men went to a Black church in East Baton Rouge, Louisiana, drove away its occupants, closed the building and whipped some of its members. The attack is known only from a private letter by an unnamed Louisiana correspondent to J. E. Bruce, the Black editor of The Exodus in Washington, which reached Northern papers in late August 1880. Northern papers reprinted it as the letter-writer offered it, as evidence of what "Democratic rule" meant for Black Southerners ahead of the presidential election.

episodes.title: Whipping of Henry Seay
episodes.summary: The whipping of Henry Seay was a night attack in August 1880 on an elderly Black farmhand in the eastern part of Hickman County, in which unnamed men took him from his cabin, whipped him and ordered him to leave the neighborhood. Seay refused to go, and warrants were issued for one or two of the men, whom he had identified. The only account found is a special dispatch in the Chicago Daily Tribune, which called it "a dastardly outrage."

episodes.title: Killing of Bonaparte Smith
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; kept as a 1880 test of the lone-actor rule (Neal 2026-11-13); attacker race: unstated
episodes.summary: The killing of Bonaparte Smith took place at the polls in Milton, Kentucky, on election day, August 2, 1880, when Smith, a Black man, was knocked down and fatally stabbed and beaten. The man who did the stabbing, whose name the papers printed as Coruman, Cornham or Cornman, was arrested. Northern and Western papers carried the news as an "election stabbing" and an "election riot", and one headed it "Nothing Like a Free Ballot."

episodes.title: Moss–Russell affair at the Library of Congress
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; kept as a 1880 test of the lone-actor rule (Neal 2026-11-13); attacker race: white
episodes.summary: The Moss–Russell affair was a fight in the Congressional library in the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., in the early summer of 1880, in which Lowell Russell, a white Democratic employee, destroyed the Garfield campaign pictures of his Black Republican co-worker John A. Moss and struck him. Moss was dismissed while Russell was restored to duty, and Russell later forfeited collateral on a charge of assaulting Moss. Republican papers treated the librarian's handling of the case as partisan injustice.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Pink Pratt
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; kept as a 1880 test of the lone-actor rule (Neal 2026-11-13); attacker race: unstated
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Pink Pratt took place near Marietta, in Cobb County, Georgia, in late August 1880, when the uncle of a white girl whom Pratt, a Black farm laborer, was accused of raping tried to shoot him as a constable arrested him. The constable took the gun away and lodged Pratt in the Marietta jail, which The Marietta Journal said was done "to keep him from being lynched." The case was reported only in that local weekly, which stated the accusation as fact and later repeated a rumor that the girl had died.

episodes.title: Halifax watermelon poisoning
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; kept as a 1880 test of the lone-actor rule (Neal 2026-11-13); attacker race: unstated
episodes.summary: The Halifax watermelon poisoning was the death of a Black man and the serious illness of five others in Halifax County, Virginia, in early August 1880, after they ate watermelons laced with strychnine from a white man's patch beside a Black religious gathering. The owner, named in a wire report as Mr. Brashe or Brash, had posted placards warning that the melons were poisoned after blaming the meeting's attendees for their disappearance. The story ran widely in the white press through August, mostly as a tale about melon stealing, and no report of an arrest or charge against the owner appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Killing of Dick Bross
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; kept as a 1880 test of the lone-actor rule (Neal 2026-11-13); attacker race: white
episodes.summary: The killing of Dick Bross was the fatal shooting of Richard "Dick" Bross, a Black man, by John Orr, a white deck-hand, in a basement tenement at 394 Clark Street, Chicago, on the night of August 28, 1880. Orr and Frank Gilbert, a Black man who had been with him, were arrested, and a coroner's jury held Orr as principal and Gilbert as accessory to murder. The Chicago Tribune followed the case for three days, and a wire dispatch carried it east as the murder of a "colored man" by a white man.

episodes.title: Killing of Alfred Perry
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; kept as a 1880 test of the lone-actor rule (Neal 2026-11-13); attacker race: unstated
episodes.summary: The killing of Alfred Perry was the fatal shooting of Perry, a Black man, by James Thorp, a workman in the Missouri Pacific railroad machine shops, at Kansas City, Missouri, on Sunday, August 22, 1880. Thorp was arrested; the wire dispatch said Perry had first made, or tried to make, an assault on him with rocks. The next afternoon, during Perry's funeral, a large Black crowd chased a man described as Thorp's brother-in-law, and white packing-house workers threatened to drive the city's Black residents into the river. The shooting ran as a brief wire item in papers across the country, while the funeral disturbance drew a separate dispatch to the Chicago Tribune.

episodes.title: Killing of Charles Haynes
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; kept as a 1880 test of the lone-actor rule (Neal 2026-11-13); attacker race: unstated
episodes.summary: The killing of Charles Haynes was the fatal shooting of Haynes, a Black man, by the attorney B. W. Moore at McKenzie, Tennessee, in late July 1880. Haynes died of the wound, and Moore was reported both to have surrendered and to have "left the country." The quarrel grew out of Haynes's interruption of Moore's speech at a barbecue.

episodes.title: Killing of Bluford Workman
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; kept as a 1880 test of the lone-actor rule (Neal 2026-11-13); attacker race: unstated
episodes.summary: The killing of Bluford Workman was the fatal shooting of a Black deaf mute man near Newberry, South Carolina, on the night of July 29, 1880. A coroner's jury found that C. D. Burton had killed him in self-defense, although the local paper had first called the killing "a horrible outrage, without the slightest provocation." Burton was later charged with the killing and released on $700 bond to await trial.

episodes.title: Killing of William Lewis (Springfield, Illinois)
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; kept as a 1880 test of the lone-actor rule (Neal 2026-11-13); attacker race: unstated
episodes.summary: The killing of William Lewis was the fatal shooting of a Black man, also called Billy Lewis, by L. W. Jamison, a horse trainer, at Jamison's house on the fair-grounds in Springfield, Illinois, on the evening of August 6, 1880. Jamison said he fired on Lewis for attempting to assault a young servant girl, and the first wire reports carried that account under headlines such as "A Would-Be Outrager Shot." After Lewis died the next day, a coroner's inquest heard that the assault story was a "pretense" and that he had been killed to conceal Jamison's relations with the girl, and Jamison and the girl were committed for murder.

episodes.title: Killing of James Kelly at Whistler, Alabama
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; kept as a 1880 test of the lone-actor rule (Neal 2026-11-13); attacker race: unstated
episodes.summary: The killing of James Kelly at Whistler, Alabama, was the fatal shooting of a Black man at a colored fair at Whistler, a few miles from Mobile, on the night of August 17, 1880. Kelly was shot by a man described as a creole, Antone Hennenberg, who escaped the next morning. The killing was known outside Alabama through a single Mobile telegraphic dispatch that ran as a one-line crime item in papers from New York to Texas.

episodes.title: Texarkana barbecue killing (1880)
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; kept as a 1880 test of the lone-actor rule (Neal 2026-11-13); attacker race: unstated
episodes.summary: The Texarkana barbecue killing was a fight at a barbecue at or near Texarkana on Thursday, August 12, 1880, in which one Black man was killed and two others were wounded. Known only from a brief Galveston News dispatch that was reprinted across the country as a one-line crime item, the report named none of those killed, wounded or involved.

episodes.title: Tyro store shooting and somnambulist killing of Uriah Phelps
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; kept as a 1880 test of the lone-actor rule (Neal 2026-11-13); attacker race: unstated
episodes.summary: The Tyro store shooting and somnambulist killing of Uriah Phelps took place in North Carolina in late July or early August 1880, when Phelps, a white storekeeper at Tyro, fired on several Black men during a dispute and was then killed in his sleep by a neighbor hired to guard against their return. Reports differed on whether Phelps's shot struck anyone, and none named the Black men. Papers across the country carried the story as a curiosity of sleepwalking, and the neighbor, O. W. Click, was discharged after a coroner's inquest and preliminary trial.

episodes.title: Stoning of Paul Smith in Correville, Ohio
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; kept as a 1880 test of the lone-actor rule (Neal 2026-11-13); attacker race: unstated
episodes.summary: The stoning of Paul Smith was an assault in Correville, a suburb of Cincinnati, Ohio, in which a man named John King threw stones at Smith, a Black man, and chased him until Smith choked him to death, probably in late July 1880. The only known account is a short wire brief that ran in a Kansas paper's crime column under the headline "Choked His Assailant to Death."

episodes.title: Killing of Bill Holmes
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; kept as a 1880 test of the lone-actor rule (Neal 2026-11-13); attacker race: unstated
episodes.summary: The killing of Bill Holmes was the fatal shooting of a Black man by John Langan at Langan's grocery store in Louisville, Kentucky, reported in a dispatch dated August 5, 1880. The only report found, a one-sentence wire item, said Holmes fired at Langan first after being told to leave, and that Langan then shot him dead.

episodes.title: Shooting of W. M. Goss
episodes.doubt: lone private attacker; kept as a 1880 test of the lone-actor rule (Neal 2026-11-13); attacker race: unstated
episodes.summary: The shooting of W. M. Goss was a nonfatal shooting near Tyler, Texas, in August 1880, in which Goss, described as "a well-to-do freedman," was shot in the breast by his son-in-law, John Jeffers. Jeffers, reported to have been drunk, was arrested by Sheriff Butler and jailed, and the shooting was noted in a single line of a state-news column.
